items.title: Join, or Die
items.note: Often called the first American political cartoon. Franklin drew the colonies as pieces of a snake to urge them to unite.

items.title: Edison’s Telephonoscope
items.note: A Victorian cartoonist imagines parents watching their daughter on a wall-sized video call, nearly 150 years early.

items.title: Drawing the Line in Mississippi
items.note: President Theodore Roosevelt refuses to shoot a captive bear. The cartoon gave the teddy bear its name.

items.title: Little Nemo in Slumberland
items.note: Nemo’s bed sprouts long legs and strolls across the city, one of the most famous pages in comics history.

items.title: Gasoline Alley
items.note: Uncle Walt wonders whether he’ll ever work up the nerve to cook the Thanksgiving turkey.

items.title: The Bosses of the Senate
items.note: Giant money bags labeled with the era’s trusts tower over the senators in the U.S. Senate chamber.

items.title: The “Brains”
items.note: Nast drew New York political boss William Tweed with a bag of money for a head. Tweed was convicted two years later.

items.title: The Modern Colossus of (Rail) Roads
items.note: Railroad magnate William H. Vanderbilt straddles the tracks, holding the reins of the nation’s railroads.

items.title: A 100% Talkie
items.note: A flapper takes a phone call on the cover of Judge, the year talking pictures took over the movies.

items.title: Puck
items.note: Puck, the impish mascot of America’s leading humor magazine, from one of its covers.
